1.title: Why Are These Rules Necessary?
1.content: Biological materials play an important role in medicine, agriculture, environmental science, biotechnology, and many other fields of research. When handled properly, microorganisms, cultured cells, environmental samples, algae, fungi, and non-vertebrate organisms can be studied safely and provide valuable scientific information. However, some biological materials can cause disease, produce harmful substances, or negatively impact the environment if handled or disposed of improperly. Professional scientists who work with biological materials receive specialized training and follow established laboratory safety procedures, institutional policies, and government regulations. Some biological materials may only be handled in laboratories that meet specific legal and safety requirements. These rules are designed to protect students, teachers, families, judges, research personnel, and the environment while helping students develop the safe and responsible laboratory practices expected of professional scientists.

2.title: Does This Project Involve Biological Materials (Excluding Live Vertebrate Animals)?
2.content: These rules apply if a project involves: . | bacteria, archaea, fungi, yeast, molds, protists, algae, or viruses; | culturing or growing microorganisms; | fermentation using microorganisms; | microbial fuel cells; | recombinant DNA techniques or genetically modified microorganisms; | cultured cells or tissues; | environmental samples such as soil, compost, wastewater, or natural water sources; | biological specimens, including blood, tissues, or body fluids; | non-vertebrate organisms, including insects, worms, crustaceans, mollusks, Daphnia, brine shrimp, planaria, hydra, or Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans); or | any other project involving biological materials other than live vertebrate animals. | . If a student is unsure whether these rules apply to their project, contact the teacher/sponsor or Regional Safety Chair before beginning the research. If the project also involves human participants or vertebrate animals, read the separate section for safety for those projects. High school students must also read and follow all applicable ISEF Safety Rules.

3.title: Before Beginning a Project, students working with Biological Materials must:
3.content: . | Read these IJAS Biological Materials Safety Rules with their sponsor. | High school students must also read and follow all applicable ISEF Safety Rules. | Discuss proper use of any AI in research with their sponsor. | Prepare all surveys, interview questions, consent forms, tests, and other materials that will be used with human participants. | Write the procedure for the experiment following all IJAS and ISEF (high school) safety rules. High School students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form 1A. | Complete a Background Research document. High School students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form1A. | Identify all biological materials that will be used and understand the potential hazards associated with them. | Determine the appropriate laboratory or research setting and ensure that appropriate adult supervision will be provided. | Learn the laboratory techniques and biosafety procedures needed to safely conduct the project. | Develop procedures for the safe handling, storage, disinfection, and disposal of all biological materials. | Ensure that they have read, and their sponsors have discussed. proper use of AI in research with them. | Prepare a written experimental procedure describing the biological materials, methods, safety precautions, and disposal procedures that will be used. | Obtain SRC approval before beginning the project when required by these rules. | Begin the project only AFTER all required paperwork and approvals have been completed. Missing, incorrectly completed, unsigned forms, or violation of any safety rules, will result in the project being disqualified by the Head Safety Judge/President. | Middle school students working with microorganisms must complete the IJAS Microorganism Endorsement Form on pg 62. | High school students working with potentially hazardous biological agents must complete the applicable ISEF Form 6A and any other required ISEF forms. Hazardous biological agents are defined as any BSL-2 agents; any bacteria, viruses, viroids, prions, rickettsia, fungi, and parasites; any Recombinant DNA (rDNA) technologies; any Biological tissues and fluids: any human or animal fresh/frozen tissues, blood, primary cell cultures, and body fluids. | Keep all completed approval forms and safety documentation with the project records and have them on the table with the project display at the science exposition. | .

4.title: General Rules for Working with Biological Materials
4.content: Sponsors are responsible for teaching students appropriate laboratory safety procedures before experimentation begins. Students working with biological materials must: . | wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), including eye protection, protective clothing, and gloves when appropriate; | wash hands thoroughly before and after handling biological materials; | use proper aseptic (sterile) technique whenever appropriate; | disinfect work surfaces before and after experimentation; | clearly label all cultures, biological materials, and containers; | safely store biological materials to prevent contamination or accidental release; | conduct biological materials research only in locations permitted by these rules and follow all laboratory safety procedures established by the school or research facility; | properly disinfect biological cultures before disposal using approved methods such as autoclaving or an appropriate sodium hypochlorite (bleach) solution; | prevent the intentional release of laboratory organisms or biological materials into the environment; and | immediately report spills, contamination, injuries, or unsafe conditions to the supervising adult. | . Unless specifically permitted under IJAS rules and conducted in an appropriately approved research laboratory under qualified supervision, students may not conduct recombinant DNA experiments or culture mammalian cells. Safety Rules for Working with Microorganisms (bacteria, archaea, fungi, yeast, molds, protists, algae, or viruses) . Projects involving microorganisms must: . | use only known, non-pathogenic microorganisms obtained from reputable commercial suppliers, educational institutions, or research laboratories; | include documentation of the source of all microorganisms with the endorsement form, research paper, and project display; | conduct microorganism research in a school laboratory or professional research facility unless the project uses only commercially obtained baker’s yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae); | NOT culture microorganisms obtained from people or other vertebrate animals, including from the mouth, nose, throat, skin, blood, body fluids, tissues, or waste; | NOT culture microorganisms collected from objects or surfaces that have been in contact with people or other vertebrate animals, including doorknobs, keyboards, telephones, countertops, eating utensils, or restroom surfaces; | NOT culture or intentionally propagate unknown microorganisms collected from environmental samples; | NOT conduct experiments using known disease-causing microorganisms or viruses unless specifically permitted under IJAS rules and conducted in an appropriately approved research laboratory under qualified supervision; | use only sealed microbial fuel cell systems; | observe mold growth studies only until visible mold growth occurs. Once visible growth is present, cultures must remain sealed and be properly disinfected and disposed of without further manipulation; and | NOT distill, concentrate, purify, or consume alcohol or other products produced during microorganism experiments when doing so creates additional safety hazards or violates applicable laws or school policies. | .

5.title: Safety Rules for Working with Non-Vertebrate Organisms
5.content: Projects involving non-vertebrate organisms must: . | minimize unnecessary injury, stress, or harm to living organisms; | provide appropriate housing, food, water, and environmental conditions whenever organisms are maintained during the investigation; | prevent the escape or intentional release of organisms into the environment; | comply with regulations governing invasive or regulated species; and | properly dispose of organisms at the conclusion of the project. | .

6.title: Special Rules for Work Done at a Certified Laboratory
6.content: If research is conducted at a certified laboratory or research facility, high school students must complete the Regulated Institution form-2C . Middle school students must include a letter from the laboratory director or supervising scientist along with the safety sheet and any appropriate endorsement form. The letter must verify that: . | the research was conducted under appropriate adult supervision; | the student followed all required laboratory safety procedures; | the laboratory is certified or otherwise authorized to conduct the research; | the supervising scientist’s name, title, and contact information are provided; and | the work described in the project was completed at that facility. | approval from the institution’s IRB and/or SRC | . Back to General Safety Rules .

8.title: The Science Project: Categories
8.content: Students must design an experiment to investigate a question or problem, design or develop a new model, computer program, solve a mathematical proof, and so forth. A project based solely on library research is not an acceptable project. The following guidelines should give one an indication of what type of experimentation or project can be done within each category and should help to place a given project in the proper category for judging. Note that building without purposeful design, testing or demonstration is not an acceptable project. A control group may not always be possible or necessary for all projects; a comparison among trials is appropriate and may be used instead. Projects in any of the listed IJAS categories below may need an endorsement sheet(s), see pages 8-9. Please make sure that all safety rules are followed, and that all endorsements are completed and displayed. Aerospace Science…is the science of the study and investigation of the Earth’s atmosphere and outer space. In the wide sense, it would include the design, manufacture, and operation of aircraft. Some topics that fall within this division are the operation of rockets, guided missiles, anything related to space travel, operation, and/or construction of satellites, observations of airflow patterns within tunnels, and the use of navigational equipment. Agriculture… involves the “implementation, production, management, and processing of agricultural commodities and services from the farm to the grocery store. It encompasses all aspects of protection and management of land and natural areas. Research that fits into this category shall be the application of scientific principles to improve the food, fiber, or fuel production or management.” Projects involving animal husbandry include the hands-on care, feeding, breeding, and management of livestock like cattle, swine, sheep, and poultry. Such projects are related to farm work, veterinary science basics, and real-world projects (from National FFA AgriScience Fair Guidelines). Astronomy…is the science dealing with all of the celestial bodies in the universe, including the planets and their satellites, comets and meteors, the stars, and interstellar matter, the star systems known as galaxies, and clusters of galaxies. Modern astronomy is divided into several branches: astrometry, the observational study of the position and motions of these bodies; celestial mechanics, the mathematical study of their chemical composition and physical condition from spectrum analysis and the laws of physics; and cosmology, the study of the universe as a whole. Behavioral Science…is the science that studies the demeanor or deportment of humans and other animals by means of observable response and the interpretation of the same as offered by the social sciences, sociology, psychology, and so forth. Some topics that fall within this division are the effect of stimuli on organisms and their responses, learning, motivation, emotion, perception, thinking, individuality, personality, and adjustment. Biochemistry…is the branch of chemistry relating to the processes and physical properties of living organisms. Topics that fall within the biochemistry division are the properties and reaction of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, enzymes, blood, urine, vitamins, hormones, poisons, and drugs. The chemistry of absorption, digestion, metabolism, respiration, and photosynthesis as organic processes also belong in this category. Botany…is the division of biology that deals with plant structure, reproduction, physiology, growth, classification, and disease. Some topics included in this category are specialization in plants, functions of various plant structures, reproduction, and heredity. Cellular and Molecular Biology…is the study of the organization and functioning of the individual cell; molecular genetics focusing on the structure and function of genes at a molecular level. Other topics may include the structure and function of the immune system, innate and acquired immunity, and the interaction of antigens with antibodies. Molecular biology concerns itself with understanding the interactions between the various systems of a cell, including the interrelationships of DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis and learning how these interactions are regulated. Chemistry…is the science that deals with structure, composition, and properties of substances and of their transformations. Topics included in this category are the composition of various compounds, the formulation of various compounds, the study of gas laws, atomic theory, ionization theory, and the analysis of organic and inorganic products. Computer Science… includes the study and development of computer hardware, software engineering, internet networking and communications, graphics (including human interface), simulations/virtual reality or computational science (including data structures, encryption, coding, and information theory). Topics in this category may include writing an original program or developing a new language and comparing them to existing ones, designing a network system, projects involving AI, testing computer speed and efficiency, overclocking, and so forth. Earth Science… is the science concerned with the origin, structure, composition and other physical features of the Earth. Some topics that fall within this division are geology (earth composition, rock formation, fossils, minerals, and fossil fuel); geography (landforms, soils, classification of streams, erosion, and sedimentation); oceanography (ocean waves, ocean currents, composition of ocean water and coastal zone management); seismology; geophysics; and meteorology. Electronics… is the branch of engineering and technology that deals with the manufacture of devices such as radios, television sets, and computers that contain electron tubes, transistors, chips, or related components. Topics in this category are circuits (electrical, digital and analog) for communication such as radio, radar, laser, transistor, television, and integrated circuits; electricity; electric motors; solar cells and amplifiers. Engineering… is concerned with the practical application of scientific knowledge in the design, construction, and operation of roads, bridges, harbors, buildings, and machinery, lighting, heating, and communication systems. Some topics in this category are stress testing of building materials, strength composition of building materials, collection of data from operating systems to compare and contrast their effectiveness. Environmental Science… is the study of the protection and care of natural resources. Topics included in this category are solar energy and its uses, water purification and usage, pollution control, soil chemistry, and insecticides. Within this area is ecology, which is the study of ecological systems, and ecological population studies. Health Science… is the study of the diseases/conditions and the health of humans, and/or the technologies associated with health. Topics to be found under this category may include anatomy, dentistry, pharmacology, physiology, pathology, ophthalmology, nutrition, sanitation, pediatrics, dermatology, neurology, allergies, speech and hearing, technical applications, and so on. May include studies using animals as models for human health studies. Materials Science… is the study of materials, nonmetallic as well as metallic, and how they can be adapted, fabricated, and/or tested to meet the needs of modern technology. Using the laboratory techniques and research tools of physics, chemistry, and metallurgy, science is finding new ways of using plastics, ceramics, and other nonmetals in applications formerly reserved for metals. Mathematics… is the science dealing with the measurement, properties, and relationships of quantities as expressed in numbers or symbols whether in the abstract or in their practical connections. Some topics included under mathematics are arithmetic (use of numbers, symbols, and numerical systems); algebra (probability, theory of equations, progressions, permutations and combinations); geometry (topology, study of geometric figures, similar figures, and scale drawings); calculus; trigonometry; statistics; and graphing. Microbiology… is the branch of biology concerned with the study of microorganisms. Topics to be found in this category are the structure and physiology of bacteria, viruses, yeasts, fungi, and protozoa, and studies involving cells or tissues in cultures. Physics… is the science that deals with the laws governing motion, matter, and energy under conditions susceptible to precise observation as distinct from chemistry or sciences dealing with living matter. Topics found in the category of physics are hydrostatic force and pressure, gravity, Newton’s Laws, relativity, kinetic theory, motion forces, work, energy, sound, light, and magnetism. Product/Consumer Science… is the study of comparisons and evaluations of manufactured or commercial products. Topics included in this category are taste tests, color preferences, quality comparisons, and product efficiency. Zoology… is the science that focuses on animals with reference to their structure, physiology, health, behavior, development, evolution, and classification. Some topics that fall within this category are structural and functional studies of vertebrates and invertebrates, reproduction, heredity, and embryology.

11.title: Why Are These Rules Necessary?
11.content: Many science and engineering projects involve chemicals, heat, flames, lasers, ultraviolet (UV) light, or other forms of energy. When used properly these materials and equipment can be handled safely. However, they can also cause burns, fires, poisoning, eye injuries, radiation exposure, or other serious harm if used incorrectly. Professional scientists receive specialized safety training before working with hazardous materials and equipment. These rules help students conduct research safely while learning the laboratory practices expected in schools, universities, and research facilities.

12.title: Does This Project Involve These Hazards?
12.content: These rules apply if a student project involves: . | chemicals or chemical reactions; | acids, bases, solvents, cleaning products, or laboratory reagents; | fuels or combustible materials; | heating or burning materials; | open flames or hot equipment; | lasers, ultraviolet (UV) light, infrared light, microwaves, or other non-ionizing radiation sources; | any procedure that could create a chemical, fire, heat, or radiation hazard. | .

13.content: . | Read these IJAS Chemical, Fire, Heat, and Radiation Safety with their Teacher/Sponsor. | High school students must also read and follow all applicable ISEF Safety Rules. | Discuss proper use of AI in research in their research project. | Write the procedure for the experiment following all IJAS and ISEF (high school) safety rules. High School Students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form 1A. | Complete a Background Research document. High School students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form 1A. | Learn how to safely use all chemicals and equipment involved in the project. | Read the Safety Data Sheet (SDS), manufacturer’s instructions, or another reliable scientific reference for every chemical used. | Understand the hazards associated with all materials and equipment that will be used. | Plan how chemicals and waste will be safely stored and disposed. | Complete the required safety sheet and any required endorsement forms. | Keep all completed approval forms and safety documentation with the project records and have it on the table with the project display at the science exposition. | . General Safety Requirements for Chemical, Fire, Heat, and Radiation Safety . These rules apply to all projects involving chemical, fire, heat, or radiation hazards. Students must: . | wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), including safety glasses whenever there is potential of eye injury; | work only under a qualified adult’s supervision required for the hazards involved; | keep work areas clean and organized; | know the location and proper use of emergency equipment, including eyewash stations, safety showers, fire extinguishers, and first aid supplies; and | immediately report spills, injuries, equipment malfunctions, or unsafe conditions to the supervising adult. | . Students may not: . | use explosive materials or explosive chemicals or intentionally create explosions; | use known carcinogens, mutagens, teratogens, or chemicals used as illegal drug precursors | obtain, possess, manufacture, or use prescription medications, controlled substances, illegal drugs, nicotine products, or cannabis products (including THC, CBD, and CBG); | intentionally produce, distill, concentrate, or purify hazardous chemical products; | use x-rays or radioactive materials; | conduct experiments that create unnecessary chemical, fire, heat, or radiation hazards. | . Note: Projects involving fermentation with baker’s yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) are covered under the Use of Biological Materials section. Any alcohol produced during permitted fermentation studies must remain incidental to the investigation and may not be distilled, concentrated, purified, or consumed.

14.title: Chemical Safety
14.content: When working with chemicals students must: . | use chemicals only for their intended purpose and according to instructions; | clearly label all chemical containers; | never mix chemicals unless the procedure specifically requires it and store incompatible chemicals separately; | avoid inhaling vapors or allowing chemicals to contact skin or eyes; | dispose of chemicals according to school, laboratory, or local regulations; and | conduct experiments involving hazardous fumes or vapors in a laboratory fume hood or another appropriately ventilated area. | .

15.title: Fire Safety
15.content: When working with combustible materials or open flames, students must: . | keep flammable materials away from ignition sources; | conduct burning procedures in a laboratory fume hood or another well-ventilated area that safely exhausts smoke and combustion products; | use open flames only when necessary and under appropriate adult supervision; | never leave an open flame unattended; | secure loose clothing and tie back long hair; | know how to extinguish fires safely; and | have appropriate fire safety equipment readily available before beginning the experiment. | .

16.title: Heat Safety
16.content: When working with hot equipment or heated materials, students must: . | use heat-resistant gloves or appropriate tools when handling hot objects; | assume heated equipment remains hot until it has cooled completely; | place hot equipment on heat-resistant surfaces; | avoid rapid temperature changes that could cause glassware to break; and | allow equipment to cool before storing or cleaning it. | .

17.title: Radiation and Light Source Safety
17.content: Projects involving lasers, ultraviolet (UV) light, infrared radiation, microwaves, or other non-ionizing radiation sources must be conducted safely and under appropriate adult supervision. Students must: . | Projects involving X-rays or radioactive materials are not permitted. | Only commercially manufactured Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3R lasers may be used. High-powered Class 3B and Class 4 lasers are not permitted. | Use radiation-producing equipment only when appropriate for the project and under qualified adult supervision; | Follow all manufacturer instructions and institutional safety requirements; | Use appropriate shielding, barriers, or enclosures when required; | Never look directly into a laser beam or aim a laser at any person or reflective surface; | Wear protective eyewear appropriate for the wavelength of the laser or UV source whenever there is a risk of eye exposure; | Wear clothing that protects exposed skin when working with ultraviolet (UV) light; and | Never intentionally expose themselves or others to lasers, ultraviolet (UV) light, infrared radiation, or other radiation sources. | .

18.title: Storage and Disposal
18.content: Students must safely store and dispose of all chemicals and hazardous materials. | Store chemicals according to the manufacturer’s instructions or the Safety Data Sheet (SDS). | Keep incompatible chemicals separated. | Clearly label all containers. | Dispose of chemicals according to school procedures and all applicable local, state, and federal regulations. | Never pour hazardous chemicals down a sink or place them in regular trash unless specifically permitted by the school or laboratory. | .

22.title: Why Are These Rules Included?
22.content: Many science and engineering projects use computers, artificial intelligence (AI), programmable devices, sensors, robotics, and electronic datasets to collect, analyze, or interpret data. When used responsibly, these technologies are valuable research tools. However, they can also create risks related to physical safety, eye strain, repetitive motion injuries, privacy, data security, and research integrity.These rules help students use technology safely, ethically, and responsibly while conducting scientific research.

23.title: Does This Project Involve These Hazards?
23.content: These rules apply if a project involves: . | using AI tools during any stage of the project; | computer programming or software development; | artificial intelligence (AI) or machine learning; | electronic or online datasets; | internet-based data collection; | programmable devices, including microcontrollers, single-board computers, robots, drones, or embedded systems; | sensors or automated data collection systems; or | extended computer use as part of the research process. | .

25.title: General Requirements
25.content: Students must: . | use computers, AI tools, datasets, and programmable devices responsibly and ethically; | follow school policies and all applicable laws; | accurately document the methods, software, AI tools, and datasets used in the project; | protect confidential or personally identifiable information; | securely store research data; and | immediately report damaged equipment, electrical hazards, or unsafe conditions to the supervising adult. | . Students may not: . | access computers, networks, or online accounts without authorization; | bypass security measures or attempt unauthorized access to computer systems; | create or distribute malicious software or intentionally damage computer systems; | falsify, fabricate, manipulate, or selectively alter research data or AI-generated results; | violate copyright, software licenses, or terms of service; or | present AI-generated work or analyses as entirely their own without appropriate disclosure. | .

26.title: Computer and Ergonomic Safety
26.content: When working on a computer for extended periods, students must: . | maintain good posture while seated; | position monitors to reduce neck strain and glare; | take regular breaks to reduce eye strain and repetitive motion injuries; | follow the 20-20-20 Rule by looking at an object at least 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes of screen use; | keep work areas organized to reduce tripping hazards from power cords and cables; and | avoid eating or drinking near computers or electronic equipment. | .

27.title: Electrical and Programmable Device Safety
27.content: Projects involving programmable devices, robotics, sensors, drones, or other electronic equipment must: . | inspect equipment for damaged cords, batteries, or components before use; | use equipment according to the manufacturer’s instructions; | disconnect power before modifying electrical circuits whenever possible; | use only power supplies appropriate for the device; | ensure moving parts do not create hazards for people or property; and | operate drones or remotely controlled devices only where permitted and under appropriate adult supervision. | .

28.title: Artificial Intelligence and Data
28.content: IJAS adopts the Society for Science/Regeneron ISEF guidelines for the use of generative artificial intelligence in student research as part of this policy. AI may be used as a supporting research tool but may not replace the student’s independent scientific reasoning, authorship, analysis, or interpretation. Students using AI or electronic datasets must: . | independently verify important facts, calculations, references, code, analyses, and other AI-generated content; | disclose substantive AI use and maintain a record of relevant prompts as required by Society for Science guidelines; | understand and be able to explain any AI-assisted code, analysis, or other material included in the project; | ensure that all interpretations and conclusions are based on the student’s own analysis; | legally obtain datasets and comply with applicable copyright, licensing, and usage restrictions; and | comply with Human Participant Safety rules whenever human data are collected or analyzed. | .

29.title: Prohibited Uses of AI
29.content: Consistent with Society for Science guidelines, students may not use AI to perform work that is required to be their own. AI may not be used to: . | write the initial research plan, abstract, research paper, poster, or substantive sections of these materials; | generate or add the student’s scientific reasoning, interpretation of results, conclusions, or future research directions; | replace the student’s own experimental design, data analysis, or understanding of the project; | substitute for reading and evaluating original sources used in the research; or | generate citations, references, or a bibliography in place of the student’s own literature research. | . AI may be used to refine student-created work where permitted by Society for Science guidelines, provided that the underlying ideas, reasoning, and scientific content remain the student’s own. AI assistance limited to grammar and syntax is permitted, provided it does not modify, add to, or replace the student’s substantive content.

30.title: AI Disclosure Statement
30.content: If artificial intelligence (AI) tools were used during any stage of the project, students must complete an AI Disclosure Statement when registering for their regional science exposition.

33.title: Contacting the IJAS Scientific Review Committee (SRC) About a Safety Concern
33.content: On this page . | Instructions for Contacting the SRC | . | After reviewing all applicable IJAS Safety Rules, if a sponsor believes that a proposed project: . | can be conducted safely, but may appear to conflict with or violate an IJAS Safety Rule; | may require special approval according to the safety rules; | involves a situation that is not clearly addressed by the IJAS Safety Rules | . The teacher sponsor must first contact the Regional Safety Chair for clarification. When contacting the Regional Safety Chair the sponsor should identify the potential rule concern and explain why the sponsor believes the project or procedure can nevertheless be conducted safely. These factors include the supervision, facilities, equipment, precautions, or modifications that would reduce or eliminate the identified risk. | If the Regional Safety Chair agrees that the project may be conducted safely but requires review because of a possible rule conflict, special circumstance, sensitive topic, or issue not clearly addressed by the IJAS Safety Rules, they must instruct the sponsor to submit the project to the IJAS Scientific Review Committee (SRC) for review before the student begins the activity in question. See “Instructions for Contacting the SRC” below. Sponsors should send the information described below to the current IJAS State Safety Chair and their Region Chair and/or Regional Safety Chair. | After reviewing the request, the IJAS SRC may: . | approve the proposed procedure; | approve the procedure with required modifications; | require additional supervision, documentation, facilities, containment, equipment, or safety precautions; | require the student to use a different procedure; or | determine that the proposed activity is not permitted under IJAS rules. | . | If modifications are required, the student must revise the procedure and submit the revised procedure for SRC review before conducting the activity. | .

34.title: Instructions for Contacting the SRC
34.content: The student’s sponsor must submit the request for review. Students and parents or guardians should not contact the Regional Safety Chair or State Safety Chair directly to request a project safety determination.The sponsor serves as the primary point of contact throughout the review process and is responsible for communicating the SRC’s determination and any required changes to the student and the student’s parent or guardian. Unless specifically authorized by the SRC, the student may not begin or resume the activity under review until the SRC has issued its determination. Include a copy of the approval on the board and in the paper of the project at the regional and state science fairs. Format for an SRC Request - Use this form . | Student / Grade / School / Region / Sponsor / Project Title | Research question / project purpose | Proposed procedure | Safety or rule concern | Relevant IJAS rule/section | Nature and level of risk | Risk-reduction measures | Student training/experience | Supervision/qualifications | Facility and safety controls | PPE / containment / ventilation / shielding | Material handling / storage / transport / disposal and emergency procedures | Procedural modifications | Experimentation status: Not begun / Procedure not yet performed / Already performed | If performed: date, location, supervision, circumstances | Specific SRC determination or approval requested | .

43.title: Why Are These Rules Necessary?
43.content: Many science and engineering projects involve electrical devices, mechanical systems, robotics, drones, motors, batteries, tools, or moving equipment. When properly designed and operated, these technologies are valuable tools for scientific investigation. However, improper use can result in electrical shock, burns, fires, cuts, crushing injuries, entanglement, or damage to people and property. These rules help students safely design, construct, test, and operate electrical and mechanical systems while developing the engineering practices used by professional scientists and engineers.

44.title: Does a Project Involve These Hazards?
44.content: These rules apply if ANY project involves: . | electrical circuits or electronic components; | batteries, capacitors, or electrical power supplies; | motors, generators, actuators, or solenoids; | robots or automated systems; | drones or other remotely operated vehicles; | mechanical devices with moving parts; | power tools or hand tools used to construct a project; | compressed springs, pneumatic or hydraulic systems; or | any equipment capable of producing electrical, mechanical, thermal, or kinetic hazards. | .

46.title: General Safety Requirements
46.content: Students must: . | work under appropriate adult supervision when using electrical or mechanical equipment; | wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), including safety glasses whenever there is a risk of flying debris, electrical failure, or eye injury; | keep work areas clean, organized, and free of unnecessary hazards; | secure long hair, loose clothing, jewelry, and other items that could become entangled in moving equipment; | use equipment only for its intended purpose and according to the manufacturer’s instructions; | disconnect power before servicing or modifying equipment whenever practical; | immediately disconnect power if equipment malfunctions or becomes unsafe; and | immediately report damaged equipment, injuries, or unsafe conditions to the supervising adult. | . Students may not: . | intentionally bypass, disable, or remove safety guards or protective devices; | operate equipment with damaged electrical cords, plugs, batteries, wiring, or mechanical components; | operate machinery without appropriate supervision; | construct or operate equipment that presents an unreasonable risk of injury to themselves or others; or | intentionally create unnecessary electrical or mechanical hazards. | .

47.title: Electrical Safety
47.content: When working with electrical systems, students must: . | use electrical components within their rated voltage, current, and power limits; | inspect wires, connectors, batteries, and power supplies before each use; | disconnect power before modifying electrical circuits whenever practical; | properly insulate exposed electrical conductors to prevent accidental contact or short circuits; | keep electrical equipment away from water or other liquids unless specifically designed for such use; | use only batteries, chargers, and power supplies recommended for the equipment; | safely charge, store, and transport rechargeable batteries according to the manufacturer’s instructions; and | immediately discontinue use of any electrical component that overheats, emits smoke, swells, leaks, or shows signs of damage. | . Students may not: . | use damaged lithium-ion or lithium-polymer batteries; | puncture, crush, disassemble, or modify batteries or their safety features; | intentionally short-circuit batteries or electrical power sources; | incorporate line voltage (120/240 VAC) into any student-built or student-modified electrical circuit unless the work is conducted in an approved laboratory under the direct supervision of a qualified adult; or | expose themselves or others to energized electrical conductors unnecessarily. | . Line voltage (120/240 VAC) refers to the electrical power supplied by standard household wall outlets. Commercially manufactured equipment and power supplies may be used according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

48.title: Mechanical Safety
48.content: Projects involving mechanical systems must: . | securely mount or stabilize equipment during operation; | keep hands, clothing, hair, and other objects away from moving parts; | use guards or protective barriers whenever rotating, cutting, pinch, or projectile hazards are present; | ensure that moving parts have completely stopped before making adjustments or repairs; | safely contain springs, flywheels, pressure vessels, or other devices that store mechanical energy; | operate equipment only within the manufacturer’s intended operating limits; and | ensure that emergency shutdown procedures are readily available whenever equipment is operating. | . Students may not: . | remove required machine guards during operation; | operate equipment that is unstable or improperly secured; | intentionally create uncontrolled mechanical hazards; or | operate equipment that could reasonably endanger participants, spectators, or property. | .

49.title: Drone Safety
49.content: Projects involving drones or other remotely operated aircraft must: . | comply with all applicable federal, state, and local laws and regulations; | operate drones only under appropriate adult supervision; | conduct flights only in locations where operation is permitted; | inspect the aircraft before each flight; | maintain a safe distance from people, buildings, vehicles, and power lines; | keep the aircraft within the operator’s visual line of sight; | immediately land the drone if unsafe conditions develop; and | respect the privacy of others when collecting photographs, video, or other data. | . Students may not: . | fly drones over people or moving vehicles; | operate drones indoors unless the location has been evaluated and approved for safe flight; | fly in restricted airspace without required authorization; or | operate drones in a reckless or unsafe manner. | .

50.title: Documentation
50.content: Students must describe in their Safety Sheet: . | the electrical, mechanical, or drone-related hazards associated with the project; | the procedures used to minimize those hazards; | the personal protective equipment (PPE) used during construction and testing; | any operating procedures, testing protocols, or emergency shutdown procedures; and | any required supervision, approvals, or specialized training. | .

60.title: Why Are These Rules Necessary?
60.content: Projects involving firearms, explosives, rockets, projectile-launching devices, or other energetic systems present some of the highest risks encountered in student research. These activities can result in serious injury or death from ballistic impact, blast pressure, fragmentation, fire, burns, or unintended launches. Because of these risks, projects involving these hazards require enhanced supervision, appropriate facilities, and, when specified below, approval by the Illinois Junior Academy of Science State Safety Review Committee (SRC) before experimentation begins.

61.title: Does a Student’s Project Involve These Hazards?
61.content: These rules apply if a project involves: . | firearms or ammunition or ballistic testing; | explosives or energetic materials; | pyrotechnics or propellants; | rockets or rocket motors; | compressed-gas launchers; | projectile-launching devices;or | any device designed to launch an object at high speed. | .

62.title: Before Beginning a Project, Students Must:
62.content: . | Read these IJAS Firearms, Explosives, Rockets, and Projectile Safety Rules with the sponsor or teacher. | High school students must also read and follow all applicable ISEF Safety Rules. | All sponsors must discuss proper use of AI in research with all of their students. | Write the procedure for the experiment following all IJAS and ISEF (high school) safety rules. High School Students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form 1A. | Complete a background research paper. High School Students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form 1A. | Determine whether the proposed project requires review and approval by the Illinois Junior Academy of Science State Safety Review Committee (SRC). | When State SRC approval is required, submit the complete proposed research procedure and all required safety documentation before beginning experimentation. | Do not begin any experimentation, testing, demonstration, or data collection requiring State SRC approval until written approval has been granted. | Conduct the project only according to the procedures approved by the State SRC. | Keep all completed approval forms and safety documentation with the project records and have it on the table with the project display at the science exposition. | .

63.title: General Safety Rules
63.content: All projects involving firearms, explosives, rockets, projectile-launching devices, or other energetic systems must: . | be conducted under the supervision of an appropriate responsible adult; | use appropriate eye protection and all other required personal protective equipment (PPE); | be conducted only in locations appropriate for the activity being performed; | maintain appropriate distances between the experiment, operators, observers, and other persons; | comply with all applicable local, municipal, state, and federal laws and regulations; | follow all applicable manufacturer instructions and recognized safety practices; and | immediately stop any activity if unsafe conditions develop. | .

64.title: State Safety Review Committee (SRC) Review and Approval
64.content: Projects involving firearms, explosives, certain energetic materials, or other activities identified in these rules as requiring additional safety review must be approved by the Illinois Junior Academy of Science State Safety Review Committee (SRC) before experimentation begins. The State SRC reviews proposed procedures to determine whether the project includes appropriate safeguards, qualified supervision, suitable facilities, and compliance with applicable IJAS safety requirements. Before beginning experimentation, the student must submit the complete proposed research procedure and all required safety documentation to the State SRC.

65.title: Firearm Safety Rules
65.content: Students May NOT: . | possess, handle, or utilize any firearm at any time while conducting a science fair demonstration or experiment; | hand-load or reload ammunition; | utilize black powder or muzzle-loading firearms; | modify or alter any firearm for experimental purposes; or | bring firearms or ammunition to any school, Regional, State, IJAS, ISAS, or ISEF Science Exposition. | . Any demonstration or experiment involving a firearm requires prior approval from the Illinois Junior Academy of Science State Safety Review Committee (SRC). When a firearm-related project is approved: . | At all times, the firearm shall be handled and the demonstration or experiment shall be conducted by a person over 21 years of age who is certified as a police officer by the Illinois Law Enforcement Training and Standards Board or by a person licensed as a Private Detective or Private Security Contractor who possesses a currently valid Firearms Control Card issued by the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation (IDFPR). A Concealed Carry License issued by the Illinois State Police or a Permanent Employee Registration Card (PERC) issued by IDFPR does not satisfy this requirement. | The student and all bystanders shall remain behind a ballistic shield and wear appropriate eye and hearing protection. | The supervising police officer or IDFPR-licensed professional shall provide a signed statement: . | describing the demonstration or experiment; | certifying that it is safe; | explaining why it is safe; and | providing copies of all required credentials. | . | The supervising police officer or IDFPR-licensed professional shall provide a Certificate of Liability Insurance in the amount of not less than $1,000,000, naming the Illinois Junior Academy of Science, Inc., as Additional Insured. | The facility where the demonstration or experiment is conducted shall provide a Certificate of Liability Insurance in the amount of $1,000,000, naming the Illinois Junior Academy of Science, Inc., as Additional Insured. | The student, parent or guardian, supervising professional, and all persons present during the demonstration or experiment shall execute any liability releases required by the Illinois Junior Academy of Science. | Only commercially manufactured firearms less than 50 years old may be used. | Only commercially manufactured fixed-cartridge ammunition manufactured in accordance with SAAMI standards may be used. | .

66.title: Safety Rules for Explosives and Energetic Materials
66.content: Students may not independently manufacture, modify, or test: . | explosives; | explosive mixtures; | improvised energetic materials; or | other materials intended to produce an uncontrolled or hazardous energetic reaction. | . Projects involving explosives, explosive mixtures, or other hazardous energetic materials require prior approval from the Illinois Junior Academy of Science State Safety Review Committee (SRC) before experimentation begins. Approved work involving these materials must: . | be conducted under appropriate professional supervision; | be conducted only at a facility appropriate for the proposed activity; | use appropriate barriers, shielding, distance, and personal protective equipment; | follow all applicable professional safety procedures; and | comply with all applicable local, municipal, state, and federal laws and regulations. | .

67.title: Safety Rules for Rockets and Projectile-Launching Devices
67.content: Projects involving rockets, rocket motors, projectile-launching devices, compressed-gas launchers, or other energetic launching systems must: . | operate only under appropriate adult supervision; | be conducted only in locations appropriate for safe operation; | maintain safe distances between operators, observers, and launch areas; | inspect all equipment before each launch or test; | secure launchers or other equipment appropriately before operation; | use appropriate barriers, shields, restraints, or other protective measures when necessary; | ensure that projectiles are directed toward an appropriate and controlled target or recovery area; | follow all manufacturer instructions and applicable safety codes; and | comply with all applicable local, municipal, state, and federal laws and regulations. | . Projects involving unusually powerful, modified, improvised, or potentially hazardous launching systems may require review by the State SRC before experimentation begins.

68.title: Model Rocketry
68.content: Model rocketry projects using commercially manufactured motors are exempt from the firearm provisions of this section. These projects must: . | be conducted under the supervision of a parent, guardian, or teacher who is at least 21 years of age; | use commercially manufactured rocket motors; | use rockets and launch systems appropriate for the commercially manufactured motor being used; | be conducted in a location appropriate for safe launch and recovery; | maintain appropriate distances between the launch area, participants, observers, buildings, roads, and other hazards; | comply with all applicable laws and regulations; and | follow recognized model rocket safety practices. | . 71.title: Why Are These Rules Necessary?
71.content: Research involving people can lead to new discoveries and help solve real-world problems. However, the safety, health, privacy, dignity, and rights of every participant must always come first. Professional researchers receive specialized training in research ethics, and their studies are reviewed by Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) to protect participants. Although student research differs from professional research, the Illinois Junior Academy of Science (IJAS) follows these same ethical principles. These rules apply whenever a project involves people in any way and includes surveys, interviews, questionnaires, observations, testing products or prototypes, measuring physical or psychological responses, recording images or video, taste testing, or asking participants to perform an activity. Lack of correctly completed, signed forms, or violation of any safety rules, will result in the project being disqualified by the State Safety Chair or the IJAS President or their representative.

72.title: Before Beginning a Project, students working with Human Participants must:
72.content: . | Read these IJAS Use and Care of Human Participant Rules with the sponsor. | High school students must also read and follow all applicable ISEF Safety Rules. | Discuss proper use of AI in research with their teacher sponsor. | Prepare all surveys, interview questions, consent forms, tests, and other materials that will be used with human participants. | Write the procedure for the experiment following all IJAS and ISEF (high school) safety rules. High School Students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form 1A. | Complete a Background Research document. High School students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form 1A. | Submit the research procedure and all participant materials to the IRB for review and approval before beginning any experimentation or data collection. | The IRB must include an educator or science teacher who is not the student’s sponsor, a school administrator (such as a principal), and a medical or mental health professional (such as a doctor, school nurse, or school psychologist). Note: To avoid conflicts of interest, the student’s Adult Sponsor, parent or guardian, or Qualified Scientist for the project cannot serve on the IRB reviewing that specific study. | The IRB may approve the project or require changes before approval is granted. | IRB members will sign the IJAS Human Endorsement Sheet (p. 58-59) for middle school students or the applicable ISEF Human Participants Form for high school students. | By signing, each IRB member confirms that they have reviewed the proposed research procedure and participant materials and, based on their professional judgment, believe that the study provides appropriate protections for the safety and welfare of the human participants and may proceed as approved. | . | Obtain the required signatures from participants and, when required, from a parent or guardian for participants under 18 years of age. | Missing, incorrectly completed, or unsigned forms, or violation of any safety rules, will result in the project being disqualified by the State Safety Chair or IJAS President or their designated representative. | Complete the required Safety Sheets and any necessary endorsement form(s). High School students must use the ISEF forms. Middle School students should use the IJAS forms on p. 56-62 of this manual. | Keep all completed approval forms and safety documentation with the project records and have it on the table with the project display at the science exposition. | .

73.title: General Rules for Working with Human Participants
73.content: All human participant research must: . | Present no greater than minimal risk than that encountered during everyday life or routine educational activities; | Obtain informed consent from all participants, unless this is waived by the IRB. | Protect participant privacy and confidentiality by collecting only necessary information, securely storing identifiable information, and reporting results without identifying participants whenever practical; | Minimize physical, emotional, psychological, social, legal, and economic risks; and | Not involve medical diagnosis, treatment, invasive procedures, bodily fluids, or administration of drugs or medical devices unless specifically permitted under separate IJAS rules. | .

74.title: Informed Consent for Human Participants
74.content: Unless waived by the IRB, before participating, participants — or their parent or legal guardian when required — must be informed of: . | the purpose of the study; | what participants will be asked to do; | any reasonably foreseeable risks and expected benefits; | how their information will be protected; and | that participation is voluntary and they may withdraw at any time without penalty. | Photographs, audio recordings, and video recordings may only be collected with appropriate consent. | . A sample consent form that may be used is found with the endorsement forms and using this link.

75.title: Safety Rules for Physical Activity Projects
75.content: Projects involving physical activity must present no greater than minimal risk. Students must: . | limit activities to those comparable to routine physical education classes or recreational activities; | Include with safety documentation that each participant has a current school physical examination on file with the school nurse or written medical clearance from a licensed healthcare provider; | provide appropriate adult supervision; and | allow participants to stop the activity at any time without penalty. | .

76.title: Safety Rules for Food and Beverage Studies
76.content: Projects involving food or beverages must protect participants from allergic reactions, foodborne illness, and other avoidable health risks. Students must: . | use only foods and beverages safe for human consumption and prepared using appropriate food safety practices; | Ingredients, amount of food or beverage and preparation method must be included on the informed consent form; | include evidence in the paper and on the display board that quantities of food and non-alcoholic beverages are limited to normal serving amounts or less and must be consumed in a reasonable amount of time. | identify participant food allergies and dietary restrictions; | not administer alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, cannabis, medications, or dietary supplements unless specifically permitted under separate IJAS rules. | .

77.title: Safety Rules for Behavioral Science Projects
77.content: Behavioral science projects involve studying human thoughts, emotions, attitudes, opinions, decision-making, behavior, or social interactions. While all human participant projects require IRB approval, additional care should be taken when a study involves sensitive topics, deception, or the potential for emotional, psychological, social, or privacy-related harm. For these projects, the IRB should pay particular attention to the level of risk involved, the wording of questions, the age and vulnerability of participants, how privacy and confidentiality will be protected, and whether participation could cause discomfort, embarrassment, distress, or other harm. Examples of sensitive topics include: . | physical or mental health; | medical conditions or diagnoses; | trauma, abuse, or neglect; | family relationships, including divorce or family conflict; | bullying, friendships, or social acceptance; | body image or self-esteem; | gender identity, sexual orientation, or sexual behavior; | political beliefs or other strongly held personal beliefs; | race, ethnicity, discrimination, or religion; | alcohol, nicotine, vaping, cannabis, or illegal drug use; | illegal activities; or | any topic that could reasonably cause embarrassment, emotional distress, social harm, or an invasion of privacy. | .

78.content: If research is conducted at a certified laboratory or research facility, high school students must complete the Regulated Institution form-2C . Middle school students must include a letter from the laboratory director or supervising scientist along with the safety sheet and any appropriate endorsement form. The letter must verify that: . | the research was conducted under appropriate adult supervision; | the student followed all required laboratory safety procedures; | the laboratory is certified or otherwise authorized to conduct the research; | the supervising scientist’s name, title, and contact information are provided; and | the work described in the project was completed at that facility. | approval from the institution’s IRB and/or SRC | . 84.title: AI Usage During Research
84.content: All sponsors are responsible for discussing the proper use of AI in research with all of their students, both middle and high school.. Generative AI may be used as a support tool in student research, but it may not replace the student’s own thinking, analysis, interpretation, or writing. Students are responsible for verifying AI-generated information and citations, documenting AI use when required, and following all applicable ISEF rules regarding acceptable and unacceptable uses of generative AI. See the full ISEF Generative AI Use Guidelines for details and examples. If a student uses an artificial intelligence (AI) tool at any stage of the project, the student must complete an AI Disclosure Statement when registering for the regional science fair. The disclosure must identify the AI tool used and explain how it was used in the project. This requirement applies to AI use during project development, experimentation, data analysis, coding, writing, editing, creation of figures or images, and preparation of presentation materials.

94.title: Aims and Objectives of the Policy and Procedure Manual
94.content: The primary aim of this manual is to communicate the information needed by the student and sponsor so that a safe and humane experimental project or paper is presented at the regional and state expositions. Please read this book carefully and resolve any questions before you enter a project or paper. The Illinois Junior Academy of Science expects all schools and regions to follow all rules, regulations, and guidelines of the state organization. The Illinois Junior Academy of Science will insist that all projects and papers entered into state competition meet all of the rules, regulations, and guidelines of the Illinois Junior Academy of Science. No arbitrary safety procedures or rules may be instituted at the regional level that will limit a school or student’s participation at a regional fair and potentially prevent a student advancing to the state level. Projects that are sent to the State Science Exposition that do not meet the rules, regulations, and guidelines of the Illinois Junior Academy of Science will be disqualified. The Board of Directors of the Illinois Junior Academy of Science will allow no exceptions to the rules and guidelines as stated in this policy and procedure manual. Safety rules are not meant to be barriers to progress that have been arbitrarily imposed to make it difficult for students to present a project. The objective of the Policy and Procedure Manual is to provide policies and procedures that are designed for the safety of the experimenter, as well as the safety of those that will judge and/or view the project.

103.title: How Do I Know If I Need a Qualified Scientist?
103.content: A Qualified Scientist is NOT required for every project. 138.title: Rules and Regulations
138.content: The student and the sponsor have ultimate responsibility for the safety of the student and test subjects while doing experiments or otherwise developing a project for the Science Exposition. 148.title: Parents
148.content: Parents are proud of the accomplishments of their son or daughter, and parents are anxious to see them succeed in this introductory phase of a possible career or a lifelong interest in science. The role of the parent is to support the child’s independent efforts, not to take over the project. The challenge is to provide just enough assistance to allow a child’s own efforts to take center stage, while offering ideas and resources that might help them raise their efforts to a higher level. Keep in mind the following suggestions: . | Review this Policy and Procedure Manual in its entirety and any other materials the child’s science teacher (sponsor) provides about the requirements of the project. All State information is available at www.ijas.org. | Encourage students as they brainstorm ideas for the project. Do not be too quick to shoot ideas down as impractical or expensive – let the student explore ideas first. If there are concerns, form them into questions for the student to consider. If possible, allow the student to rule out impractical ideas before the parent does. | Parents must understand what is required before approving a science project topic. Will it be able to be accomplished with all the other activities that students are involved in, along with other academic requirements? | Support the child in researching the topic and conducting the experiment; assist by supplying transportation (if needed), and access to information and materials. Often excellent learning opportunities will present themselves. Parents could teach the child to use a piece of equipment or machinery rather than doing it for the chld just because it might be easier. | It is recommended that parents become familiar with the safety guidelines and see that they are followed. See pp 7-33. Some projects may be disqualified if these projects are done at home. | Assist a student in thinking through experimental or design procedures and how they plan to record and organize their data. | Students might need assistance in preparing their display board and presentation. 151.title: Why Are These Rules Necessary?
151.content: The basic aim of experiments involving animals is to achieve an understanding of life processes and to further society’s knowledge. Experiments requiring the use of vertebrates must have a clearly defined objective, investigate a biological principle, and/or answer a scientific inquiry. Such experiments must be conducted with a respect for life and an appreciation of humane considerations. To the degree possible, students should be cautioned about doing projects that involve vertebrates. However, if the teacher and the student feel that vertebrates must be used, the following rules must and will apply. It is strongly recommended that living organisms such as plants, bacteria, fungi, protists, worms, snails, insects, or other invertebrates be used. Their wide availability, simplicity of care, and subsequent disposal make them very suitable for student work. These rules are designed to protect vertebrate animals while helping students develop the humane and responsible research practices expected of professional scientists. Projects that do not follow these rules may be disqualified from the Illinois Junior Academy of Science (IJAS) Science Fair.

152.title: Does a Project Involve Non-Human Vertebrate Animals?
152.content: These rules apply if a project involves: . | mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish; | chicken or other bird embryos; | maze running, learning, conditioning, or behavioral studies involving vertebrate animals; | changing the environment, diet, housing, or other conditions of a vertebrate animal; or | any other experimentation involving a living non-human vertebrate animal. | . If a student or teacher sponsor is unsure whether these rules apply to a project, students should contact their teacher sponsor. The teacher sponsor must clarify questions with the Regional Safety Chair before students begin research. If a project involves human participants, microorganisms, biological materials, or non-vertebrate organisms, read the separate section for safety for those projects.

153.title: Before Beginning a Project, Students Must:
153.content: . | Read these IJAS Use and Care of Non-Human Vertebrate Animals with their sponsor. | High school students must also read and follow all applicable ISEF Safety Rules.All sponsors must discuss proper use of AI in research with all of their students. | Prepare all surveys, interview questions, consent forms, tests, and other materials that will be used with human participants. | Write the procedure for the experiment following all IJAS and ISEF (high school) safety rules. High School Students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form 1A. | Complete a Background Research document. High School students will use this in their ISEF Research Plan form 1A. | Clearly define the objective of the investigation; | Ensure that the project investigates a biological principle and/or answers a scientific inquiry; | Consider whether plants, microorganisms, protists, worms, snails, insects, or other invertebrates could be used instead; | Develop procedures that respect life and humane considerations; | Obtain any required approval for Special Circumstances/Exceptions; and | Begin a project only AFTER all required paperwork and approvals have been obtained and completed. | Complete the Non-Human Vertebrate Endorsement Form with a sponsor prior to experimentation; | . No non-human vertebrate projects will be allowed that are in violation of these rules. No person may perform an experiment for the student that violates these rules, and no person may give permission for a project that violates these rules except in approved Special Circumstances/Exceptions.

154.title: General Care Requirements
154.content: Students and sponsors working with non-human vertebrate animals must: . | provide proper care in well-ventilated and properly lighted locations; | provide proper nutrition; | maintain proper temperature; | provide adequate water; | maintain sanitary surroundings; | ensure that organisms are properly cared for during weekends and vacation periods; and | conduct all experimentation with respect for life and an appreciation of humane considerations. | . The student and the sponsor are responsible for ensuring that all animals receive proper care throughout the investigation.

155.title: Working with Behavioral, Learning, or Conditioning Studies
155.content: Projects involving maze running and other learning or conditioning activities must: . | not withhold food or water for more than 24 hours; and | not withhold food or water from an animal with a high metabolic rate for a length of time that would produce undue stress on the animal. | . Behavioral studies must follow all other applicable non-human vertebrate animal rules.

156.title: Working with Chicken or Other Bird Embryos
156.content: Chicken or other bird embryo projects are allowed, but: . | experimental treatment must be discontinued at or before 72 hours before the scheduled hatch day; and | Seventy-two hours before the scheduled hatch day time or before, the egg must be destroyed. | . Projects involving behavioral studies of newly hatched chickens or other birds are allowed if no changes have been made in the normal incubation and hatching of the organism and all vertebrate animal rules are followed. Only non-manipulated eggs may be hatched.

157.title: Cultures from Vertebrate Animals
157.content: Projects involving cultures from warm-blooded animals must follow the applicable Biological Materials rules. No primary or secondary cultures involving warm-blooded animals may be taken: . | directly from the mouth, throat, skin, or other parts of the animal; or | indirectly from cage debris, droppings, countertops, or similar materials or surfaces. | . Primary or secondary cultures include the growth of microorganisms, tissue cells, or other living matter in a specially prepared nutrient medium. Cultures purchased from reputable biological supply houses or research facilities are suitable for student use when conducted according to the applicable microorganism rules. These Actions Are Not Allowed When Working with Vertebrate Animals that: . | use invasive or pain-producing procedures, including surgery, injections, blood collection, burns, or electrical stimulation; | subject animals to undue stress, pain, injury, or risk of death; | administer over-the-counter, prescription, illegal drugs, or alcohol to measure their effects; | make potentially harmful environmental changes without prior approval; | withhold food or water long enough to cause undue stress or for more than 24 hours in learning/conditioning studies; | prepare primary or secondary cultures from warm-blooded animals or materials contaminated by them; | experimentally manipulate bird embryos within 72 hours of hatching or hatch experimentally manipulated eggs. | .

161.title: Writing a Research Paper for a Science Investigation
161.content: Scientists, regardless of their level of achievement, are only as effective as their ability to communicate to others, in spoken or written word, the results of their endeavors. A scientific paper is, very simply, a clearly written, concise report of an experimental research project. Three copies of the paper are required for Poster Session and two copies of the paper are required for Paper Session. References and embedded citations follow APA format; however, charts, graphs, tables, etc. do not have to follow APA format.

162.title: Technical Points of a Research Paper
162.content: In preparing the paper, the author should be concerned with the following mechanics: . | The paper must be typed, doubled spaced and have at least one-inch margins on standard 8 ½” X 11” paper. | Printed pages may be double-sided. | The font and type size must be appropriate for a scientific paper: for example, 12 pt. Times New Roman. | Correct grammar and spelling are evident. | The paper must be neat and legible. | The primary scientist’s last name is in the upper right-hand corner of each page after the Table of Contents. | Graphs should be suitably titled and have all axes correctly labeled. Do not forget to include the correct units of measurement for any numbers. | Photographs should be of good quality and contrast and should have captions typed with them. | .

163.title: The Physical Arrangement of the Written Report of the Experimental Investigation
163.content: The following section establishes the basic written report requirements. Familiarity with the basic techniques and requirements will help students read and understand scientific publications, give a view of how scientists think, and help students write their own scientific paper that describe and explain results of the research investigation. Keep in mind, students must think before writing, then rethink, revise, rewrite, and reread again and again. Make it clear and concise. The paper must include (in this order): . | Abstract - Use the IJAS Abstract form, https://ijas.org/rules . | The abstract is a concise summary of the work and the first sheet of the research paper, it will help the reader form an opinion of the work. Students will find writing and rewriting will help produce a good short summary of the project in the required form. | The physical form of the abstract is as follows: typed single-spaced, limited to 250 words or fewer, and limited to three paragraphs - purpose, procedure, conclusion. | . | Title Page - The title should be concise and clear. A scientific title includes the independent and dependent variable. | Table of Contents - Include subsection name and page numbers. | Acknowledgements – Give credit to those who have given guidance, materials, and/or use of facilities. | Purpose and Hypothesis – State precisely the question that is being investigated. Include the hypothesis or the expected outcome of the testable question. Use If/Then/Because format when feasible. | Background Research – Report the background information and/or work done in the past that pertains to the investigation. These references should be properly documented and listed on the Reference List. Traditional footnotes are not to be used for citing references. | Materials and Methods – A simple step-by-step account of what was done and must be clear and detailed enough so that the reader can duplicate the work. The apparatus and materials used should be listed. Explain the workings of any apparatus constructed or used. Drawings, diagrams that are clearly labeled, and photographs are appropriate if they enhance and clarify students’ explanations, but do not use them as filler. | Results and Discussion – . Data . | Data are to be organized in tables and/or figures with graphic presentations that are easily read by someone not familiar with the work. All data should be listed, when possible. Summary data should follow the raw data. | Choosing the appropriate type of graph is important. Graphs should be presented so that someone not familiar with the work easily reads them. Axes should be labeled with titles and correct units of measurement in metric when appropriate. | If quantitative data are not involved, a day-by-day log may be used in place of tables and charts. In either case, care should be taken to ensure accuracy and clarity. | . Data Analysis and Discussion . | The results section should also include a description and explanation of figures and tables. | Discussion should include an evaluation and interpretation of the data and/or results of investigation, and comparison of the experimental data to what others have found. | . Error Analysis . | Finally, experimental and/or measurement errors potentially affecting the conclusion have been considered and are discussed. Ways in which error was/could have been avoided may also be addressed. | . | Conclusion – This should be a concise evaluation and interpretation of the data and/or results. The conclusion should be limited to the results of the investigation and should refer back to the stated purpose and hypothesis. Internal citations from references used in the Background Research are encouraged. | Reference List - This is a list of published articles, books, and other communications actually cited in the paper. Sources should be current. The reference list section is arranged alphabetically according to the author/editor’s last name when it is known or the first significant word in the title if the author/editor is not known. The correct style to use for citing references in the reference list section is discussed in detail in the APA, 7th Edition. | .

164.title: The Physical Arrangement of the Written Report of the Design Investigation
164.content: The following section establishes the basic written report requirements. Familiarity with the basic techniques and requirements will help students read and understand scientific publications, give an inside view of how scientists and engineers think, and help students write their own scientific paper that describes the results of their research investigation. The main point to keep in mind is to think before writing, then rethink, revise, rewrite, and reread again and again. The objective is to make the writing clear and concise. The paper must include (in this order): . | Abstract - Use the IJAS Abstract form, https://ijas.org/rules . | The abstract is a concise summary of students’ work and the first sheet of the research paper, it will help readers form an opinion of the work. Students will find writing and rewriting will help produce a good, short summary of the project in the required form. | The physical form of the abstract is as follows: typed single-spaced, limited to 250 words or fewer, and limited to three paragraphs - Purpose, Procedure, Conclusion. | . | Title Page - The title should be concise and clear. A scientific title includes the independent and dependent variable if feasible.. | Table of Contents - Include subsection name and page numbers. | Acknowledgements – Give credit to those who have given guidance, materials, and/or use of facilities. | Problem or Need – Precisely state the question being investigated. Include a discussion of the problem or the need and the expected outcome of the testable question. | Background Research – Report the background information and/or work done in the past that pertains to the investigation. These references should be properly documented and listed on the Reference List.
